messages.subject: QMET in ectotherms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

My apologies if it is a bit of a naive question, but I was just wondering where the 0.0056 factor came from to convert respiration rate (VO2=ml/hr) to heat produced? (ie; lines 93, 99, 107 in https://github.com/mrke/NicheMapR/blob/master/src/MET.f )

I couldn't find any direct mention of it in Kearney et al. (2020), Gates (1980) or Andrews & Pough (1985).

Also, is it something we should try and customise for our study species?

All the best,
Matt

messages.subject: Re: QMET in ectotherms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

It's based on the assumption that, to a rough approximation, 1 ml O2 consumed represents about 20 J energy. The equation referred to on those line you mentioned are for ml O2 / h and watts is J / s hence the conversion factor of 0.0056 for that particular equation to go from ml O2 / h to W.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Fortran version
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

It is essentially Fortran77 with some Fortran90/95 features. It uses modules and dynamically allocated arrays which are Fortran90 features.

Main thing is that the code is fixed-format in that it allows lines only of a certain length that must start a tab in. You shouldn't have any trouble if you simply modify the existing code. I use Simply Fortran as a programming environmnet.

All the best,
Mike

But the endoR function certainly allows you to simulated death from heat stress, when a burrow would be needed, etc. You can also work out how much energy and water would be needed for thermoregulation at a snapshot in the organism's life cycle - a 'static energy budget'. The DEB model allows you to simulate the energy budget in terms of growth, development and reproduction over the whole life cycle of the animal. messages.subject: Re: Micro_USA Issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike!

Thanks for the quick response!

It seems like I at least figured out a work around for the issue. After uninstalling and reinstalling all my r files and packages and still getting the same error, I did some digging and found this https://github.com/Unidata/netcdf-c/issues/1299. With all my libraries and packages up to date, the below code still wont work:

nc <- RNetCDF::open.nc <http://open.nc>(paste0(baseurl, "tmmn_1979_CurrentYear_CONUS.nc"))

However, this code works just fine:

nc <- RNetCDF::open.nc <http://open.nc>(paste0(baseurl, "tmmn_1979_CurrentYear_CONUS.nc#fillmismatch"))

Given that, I went into my version of micro_usa()  and suffixed that #fillmismatch onto any instance of it calling data from the 1979_CurrentYear_CONUS database. Everything's back up and working for me now!
Unsure if this is a consistent issue with the most updated versions of RNetCDF, something from the data provider, or if my computer is just having its own issues, but maybe this will be helpful somewhere down the line!

Best,

Connor

messages.subject: Re: EndoR Clarification
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,
You're not missing anything - you do indeed have to adapt your own code to program in your own behavioural responses. One way to do this is to dynamically vary the behaviour each hour, e.g. by trying different options and choosing the best (e.g. selection of shade and or going under ground). Or, you run a number of scenarios in advance for all time periods and then subsequently process the results to work out what would be the best behavioural option. The latter is more intensive but has the advantage that you could play around with different behavioural priorities and not have to keep running the model other than the initial run.
Hope that helps,
Mike

messages.subject: How did the parameters Usrhyt and Climb interact?
messages.subject_clean: How did the parameters Usrhyt and Climb interact?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone, I hope this email finds you in good health.

--I sincerely request your help in solving a question, What does suppose to biologically mean if I set a reference height (Usrhyt) of 3cm in the micro_ncep model, along with the option that the simulated lizard can climb to thermoregulate in the ectotherm model?

--Now, if I'm right, the climbing parameter allow the simulated lizard to move vertically to microhabitats up to 120 cm above ground. And that microclimates are cooler at higher heights.

--Then, the answer to my question could be that (i) the lizard experiences the microclimate simulated at 3 cm of height at any perch height up to 120 cm, thus, the thermoregulation by climbing is impractical? or that (ii) the lizard experiences different microclimates at each perch height and thus it climbs to the perch height that better allow it to thermoregulate; i.e., the thermoregulation by climbing works.

--To find out we run the ectotherm model at 10 geographic points as a pre-test, we set the models at 3 cm or 120 cm above the ground, allowing the simulated lizard to climb or not, therefore we run the model four times, as many as the treatments: 3cm climbing and not-climbing and 120 cm climbing and not-climbing (table below).
--I found that the mean body temperature of the simualted lizard was warmer at 3 cm than at 120 cm, either when the lizard was allowed to climbing or not (table columns). Besides that the mean body temperature was cooler when the lizard was allowed to climbing than when not, at both perch heights (table rows).

Heights         Climbing Not-climbing    Difference
3 cm         32.7         33.6             0.9
120 cm         31.4         32.5             1.2
Difference   1.4           1.1

Therefore, even when the reference height was 3 cm, the simulated lizard could reach cooler microclimates by climbing (3 cm row), thus the microclimates should differ at each perch height and the second answer should be right, isn't it?
But if a simulated lizard set at 3cm of perch height can reach the microclimate at 120 cm by climbing (climbing column), Why the simulated lizard set at 120 cm above ground still resulting with cooler body temperatures.

Thank you very much in advance for your valuable help. The script and data needed to reproduce my results are attached.

messages.subject: Re: How did the parameters Usrhyt and Climb interact?
messages.subject_clean: How did the parameters Usrhyt and Climb interact?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Israel,
The 'climber' option adds the possibility for the animal to go to the height specified by Refhyt in the microclimate model. The latter height is the 'reference height' at which the forcing weather/climate data is provided for the microclimate model, specifically air temperature, relative humidity and wind speed. In the micro_ncep function,  Refhyt is 2 m. This variable is not a user's choice - it is determined by the height of the weather stations used for the input weather/climate data. The Usrhyt parameter is one you can change depending on your organism, and is the height at which the animal is at normally when foraging. There are equations that can infer the air temperature, wind speed and relative humidity at the Usrhyt from the Refhyt. When you specify 'climber=1', the ectotherm model will use climbing as a last resort after exhausting postural changes and shade seeking (if these are turned on). So if you set the Usrhyt to 3 cm and climber = 1, you'll see it jump up to the 2m environment if it's getting too hot or too cold at 3 cm. This will put it in a windier environment but also a cooler environment during the day (but a warmer environment during the night). If you turn off shade seeking and burrowing you'll see the animal climb a lot depending on how hot/cold the microclimate near the ground is relative to their specified behavioural thermoregulatory thresholds. Note that climbing is prioritised over burrowing. So once it gets too hot (or cold) climbing it will, as the final option, go under ground.
All the best,
Mike

The latter height is the 'reference height' at which the forcing weather/climate data is provided for the microclimate model, specifically air temperature, relative humidity and wind speed. In the micro_ncep function,  Refhyt is 2 m. This variable is not a user's choice - it is determined by the height of the weather stations used for the input weather/climate data. The Usrhyt parameter is one you can change depending on your organism, and is the height at which the animal is at normally when foraging. There are equations that can infer the air temperature, wind speed and relative humidity at the Usrhyt from the Refhyt. When you specify 'climber=1', the ectotherm model will use climbing as a last resort after exhausting postural changes and shade seeking (if these are turned on). So if you set the Usrhyt to 3 cm and climber = 1, you'll see it jump up to the 2m environment if it's getting too hot or too cold at 3 cm. This will put it in a windier environment but also a cooler environment during the day (but a warmer environment during the night). If you turn off shade seeking and burrowing you'll see the animal climb a lot depending on how hot/cold the microclimate near the ground is relative to their specified behavioural thermoregulatory thresholds. Note that climbing is prioritised over burrowing. So once it gets too hot (or cold) climbing it will, as the final option, go under ground.
> All the best,

> You're not missing anything - you do indeed have to adapt your own code to program in your own behavioural responses. One way to do this is to dynamically vary the behaviour each hour, e.g. by trying different options and choosing the best (e.g. selection of shade and or going under ground). Or, you run a number of scenarios in advance for all time periods and then subsequently process the results to work out what would be the best behavioural option. The latter is more intensive but has the advantage that you could play around with different behavioural priorities and not have to keep running the model other than the initial run.
